Avec <em>Une exposition de Marven Clerve: With Une exposition de Marven Clerveau : Visions Hip-Hop QC, on view from February 11 to March 26 at Centre Phi, the multidisciplinary artist invites us not only to discover his creations, but also to step into the little-known world of music.
Au fil d’un parcours jalonné de 20 portr: Along a path marked by 20 large-format portraits of Quebec hip-hop figures, the mixed-media works carry us into the musical and entrepreneurial worlds of local artisans. The exhibition includes audiovisual installations, archival documents, and events and workshops where the public can get acquainted with art and music. “This is research and creation that you’re discovering with me,” says the 26-year-old artist, who is taking on a project of this scale for the first time.
« Je suis un artiste multidisciplinaire,: “I’m a multidisciplinary artist, I do a bit of everything, I like exploring new things,” explains the self-taught artist from his home in Montréal-Nord. While this new series of works combines painting and collage techniques, in his artistic practice Mr. Clerveau also makes manga-style comics and is currently working on a book. He is also a fan of abstraction and cites Basquiat as an inspiration. The artist is also in the habit of painting himself, an approach he shares with Frida Kahlo, with whom he feels a certain kinship. “There’s one self-portrait that spoke to me,” he says, describing the Mexican artist’s The Broken Column (1944), in which a metal column runs through Frida Kahlo’s body. “I’m an artist who lives with scoliosis. When I was 12, I had a major operation: they put a rod in my spine,” explains Marven Clerveau, who drew on the work to create Disphl’Égo, an autobiographical series. With Visions Hip-Hop Qc, Marven is no stranger to portraits. “I often drew famous artists, often American ones,” he says, citing his own musical references and those of the people around him.
Il travaillait sur des toiles de Tupac,: He was working on canvases of Tupac, Nas, Biggie and Aaliyah. One day, a conversation with an artistic adviser steered him in a new direction. “He said to me: ‘Why don’t you do portraits of Quebec rappers?’ It’s thanks to this project that I started following what’s being done here,” the artist recalls. What followed was exhaustive research and many meetings, as part of an inclusive approach, to represent each artist, their reality and their story faithfully. “There are also the rappers who’ve left and been forgotten,” Mr. Clerveau points out. He also spoke with loved ones of those who have passed away or stepped back from music. Visions Hip-Hop QC is also a tribute to those who are still around. “For those who grew up in Montréal, especially young people, I thought it was important to show how rap began and who the rappers are that we have,” says the artist, who wanted to introduce audiences to local talent. “It’s easier to talk about Tupac and Biggie.” Mr. Clerveau praises the collaborative work that allowed the project to come to life. He credits the contributions of Vladimir Delva, guest curator, DJ Gayance, who composed the soundtracks, and George Fok, who provided the visual archives. “I want to make a sequel collectively, so that this project continues,” says the artist, adding that he has many more hip-hop figures to paint.
La pochette de l’album Gansta, de Dice B: The cover of Dice B’s album Gansta, by Marven Clerveau
« Le dessin a toujours été ma passion »,: “Drawing has always been my passion,” says the self-taught artist. He tells us how, as a child, he would sit in the living room with paper and pencils to watch cartoons, which he would then draw. “It was part of a need, to feel better. I was growing up in an environment where I had a lot of difficulty,” says Mr. Clerveau, who lives with dysphasia, a language disorder. “I heard more about my weaknesses than my strengths,” he says of his school years. “I try to express myself through my art, to bring out emotion. I’m not someone for whom it’s easy to express myself by communicating directly. I express myself better with my hands, my pencils, my brushes,” he explains. Yet, fuelled by his passion, he doesn’t let himself be discouraged. “When I was in high school, I kept saying I wanted to become a visual artist,” he remembers. His teachers preferred that he keep his feet on the ground. “I was told it wasn’t a real job, and that there weren’t really any in Montréal.” So much so that he once considered moving to New York or Miami to become a painter, having grown up in Rivière-des-Prairies and Montréal-Nord. Today, he would rather show them the path he has drawn for himself.
À la suggestion d’un accompagnateur scol: At the suggestion of a school support worker, the young artist signed up for visual arts workshops. Everything changed for young Marven, who was introduced to painting, explored other artistic avenues and took part in group exhibitions. “In the beginning, I was often categorized as a person with a disability. I wanted to explore and be like everyone else,” he says. He later became a member of Diversité artistique Montréal (DAM), an organization that supports immigrant and racialized artists in their professional development. “As soon as I met these artists and the organization, I realized that in Montréal, there are lots of visual arts projects, lots of interesting things to do. It’s hard not to find them,” he says. Through mentorship, he received advice from more experienced artists, such as sculptor <l1>Bismark Villacrés</l1>, multidisciplinary artist<l2> Moridja Kitenge Banza</l2> and painter<l3> Chlag</l3>.
« Ça m’a permis de rencontrer des gens q: “It allowed me to meet people who share the same passion and to learn what the visual art world looks like,” says the artist. By extension, it was also thanks to DAM that the idea for Visions Hip-Hop Qc took root. In 2020, riding the momentum of his portraits, Mr. Clerveau teamed up with Vladimir Delva, a hip-hop artist, historian and author of the book Le boss du Québec, which traces the origins of Quebec hip-hop. Their collaboration grew stronger, and Mr. Delva, who also performs under the name Kapois Lamort, serves as curator of the exhibition at Centre Phi. “It made the project stronger and allowed us to bring in his vision. When two people work together, you get the best possible result,” says Mr. Clerveau.
Marven Clerveau a reçu une <l1>bourse Vi: Marven Clerveau received a <l1>Vivacité grant from the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec</l1> to develop his project. To get to work, he looked for a studio close to home, without success. “It’s hard to find a studio in Montréal-Nord. Yet there are plenty of artists. At the Henri-Bourassa library, which isn’t far from my place, there are often exhibitions,” he points out.
Avec l’assistance qu’il obtient pour ses: With the support he received for his research, he decided to rent a space in Hochelaga-Maisonneuve. The trip took him an hour by public transit. Still, he has fond memories of the studio he shared with three other artists. He plans to do it again, perhaps for another project, and perhaps at home in Montréal-Nord this time.
L’heure est aux célébrations pour l’arti: It’s a time of celebration for the artist. His exhibition marks a turning point in his career. With music, he is venturing into a field that is less familiar to him. “One of the reasons I wanted to move toward the hip-hop scene was also to explore. I’ve often made art that spoke about my story, about dysphasia and scoliosis; I wanted to move toward subjects I love and appreciate, to look around me at what’s happening in the world, in Montréal,” he says. While he draws inspiration from what resembles him, Marven Clerveau also has everything it takes to inspire those who resemble him. That is, in fact, what he would tell them: “You have to have more confidence in yourself, not listen too much to your ego. When you have a goal, you have to think about it positively.”
Au fil du parcours, il vaut mieux y alle: Along the way, it’s best to proceed by trial and error. “In life, there are ups and downs; you have to go with plan B if plan A doesn’t work,” he advises. “There are plenty of options; you have to believe in yourself and go at it with heart if it’s something you truly enjoy. You have to go for it.”
